newsitem.title: USA: U.S. to evacuate thousands more from N. Iraq.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to evacuate thousands more from N. Iraq.

text.p: The State Department said on Monday it was planning to evacuate thousands more Kurds and others to the United States from northern Iraq, because they were at risk from Iraqi President Saddam Hussein.

Spokesman Glyn Davies said some 5,000 people -- employees of U.S.-linked non-governmental organisations (NGOs) and their families -- would be taken to neighbouring Turkey and then flown to the Pacific Ocean island of Guam for processing to enter the United States.

The move follows the pattern of two previous evacuations from Western-protected northern Iraq. About 2,100 aid workers employed by the U.S. government were taken out in September, followed last month by some 600 Iraqi opposition figures.
Davies said the latest group consisted of employees of 24 NGOs that were either U.S.-funded or U.S.-based, or both, together with immediate family members.

The airlifts followed a move by Iraqi forces at the end of August into northern Iraq -- an area from which they had been banned since soon after Baghdad lost the 1991 Gulf War -- in support of one of two rival Kurdish factions fighting there.

Although most of the Iraqi troops are believed to have left the area, the incursion ended the Western military presence on the ground there and was seen to put at risk anyone associated with the United States.
U.S. NGOs hailed Monday's announcement. "We welcome it," said David Shorr of the Washington-based Refugees International, which has campaigned on behalf of the aid workers.

"It's been a little bit of a long time in coming, but we have felt that it's important to uphold the idea that the United States stands by those who are at risk for their association with an American effort," he said.
Davies said discussions were under way on the practical details of the evacuation with Turkey, a NATO ally which shares a border with Iraq, and it was hoped the flights would begin in a few weeks.
Once in Guam, a U.S. territory, the aid workers will be processed for entry into the continental United States.
Washington had come under considerable pressure from relief organisations and the media to do something about the NGO employees.
U.S. officials had said until now they were studying the situation, and State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said last month the employees did not appear to be in imminent danger.

But Davies said on Monday: "I think they've always been in a serious enough degree of danger that some action needed to be taken ... In essence, the situation for them hasn't gotten better. So we decided, on balance, that since we can do it, we should do it."

Explaining U.S. priorities in the evacuations, he said: "First at risk were those who actually had ID cards that said, I work for Uncle Sam. Second at risk were those who were with the Iraqi opposition ... But third at risk are these people who work for organisations that are tied to the United States."
Davies said the delay in evacuating the latest group was also partly caused by the complexity of establishing who would be involved, given that two dozen aid agencies were involved.
Many NGO workers fled their towns in the mountainous region when Saddam's troops entered the area at the invitation of the Kurdistan Democratic Party.
